Theme

Civic life: news, government & the law

surrender noun

also capitulation, capitulate, give oneself up, surrender (to the enemy), force to surrender

classical

Caes. BG 1.27: dē dēditiōne (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 188

dēditiō, dēditiōnis f.

noun, third declension

a surrender, a capitulation

Other words

  • sē dēdere — to surrender, give oneself up

    dēdō, dēdere, dēdidī, dēditum, with the reflexive; the victor in the dative · also used · classical · Caes. BG 2.15.2: Ambiānī sē suaque omnia sine morā dēdidērunt (Lewis & Short); Traupman 188

  • in dēditiōnem venīre — to surrender, come to terms of surrender

    also used · classical · Caes. BC 3.99.3 (Lewis & Short s.v. dēditiō); Traupman 188

Examples

  • populum in dēditiōnem venīre cōgere

    to force a people to surrenderTraupman 188

  • Triennium mīlitiam explēvī antequam nostrī sociīque coēgērunt Germānōs in dēditiōnem venīre.

    I completed a three-year tour of duty before our men and our allies forced the Germans to surrender.Traupman 183

  • hostem in dēditiōnem venīre cōgere

    to force an enemy to surrenderTraupman 388

See also siege, war, weapon.

SourcesLewis & Short: deditio · Lewis & Short: dedo

John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 183, 188, each phrase checked against the searchable text of the book.

Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
